item.title: Depth-resolved magnetization dynamics in Fe thin films after ultrafast laser excitation
item.description: arXiv:2603.11913v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We performed time-resolved x-ray resonant magnetic reflectivity measurements on a laser-excited ferromagnetic Fe thin film to simultaneously probe the transient magnetic and structural depth profiles with nanometer spatial and femtosecond temporal resolution. Our results show that during the first picoseconds after optical excitation, the magnetization of the Fe layer is strongly inhomogeneous, especially in the vicinity of the buried interface. By comparing our experimental results to predictions based on the microscopic three-temperature model and simulations of laser-induced spin-currents, we demonstrate that local and non-local angular momentum transfer phenomena take place simultaneously. After a few picoseconds, the magnetization relaxes back to equilibrium while the total thin film thickness starts oscillating periodically, with a maximum dilation of approximately 1.3% of the entire thin film thickness due to laser-induced stresses.

item.title: Endowing phase-field fracture models with custom strength criteria
item.description: arXiv:2606.06169v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: By now, several approaches have been proposed to endow phase-field fracture models with the ability to describe crack nucleation under multiaxial stress states. These include techniques for splitting the free energy, direct modifications of the phase-field driving or resisting forces, and the introduction of additional internal variables, such as plastic strains or other nonlinear strains. In this paper, we propose a fundamentally different strategy for incorporating arbitrary elastic domains into phase-field fracture models, formulated within the energetic framework of generalized standard materials. The proposed approach relies on letting the dissipation potential depend on the current state of the material. In this way, the elastic degradation and the strength criterion remain two distinct and independently controllable aspects of the material response, while the governing equations directly descend from a local stability condition and energy balance. Simple yet representative models are presented and thoroughly discussed to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methodology. The resulting evolution of the elastic domain is investigated in both strain and stress spaces under proportional and non-proportional loading paths, with the latter highlighting the path dependence of the dissipated work. Moreover, numerical simulations demonstrate a range of crack nucleation processes under multiaxial loading conditions for various analytical strength surfaces. The present work paves the way for future developments and applications in several directions, including crack propagation studies and dedicated numerical solution strategies.
item.dc:creator: Roberto Alessi, Matteo Brunetti, Roshan Udaram Patil, Jacinto Ulloa

item.title: Facet-Driven Electronic Modulation in Self-Aligned Phosphorus Nanoarrays
item.description: arXiv:2606.18907v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Two-dimensional (2D) materials often require specific substrate terminations for epitaxial stabilization, yet the search for suitable templates has largely focused on low-index metal surfaces, which may not provide the optimal conditions for the growth of new phases. Here, we show that crystal-facet engineering on curved Cu surfaces enables the stabilization, within a single preparation step, of two distinct phosphorus surface phases with different electronic properties. Hexagonal phosphorus adlayer forms on Cu(111) terraces, whereas a previously unreported skewed-square P overlayer is stabilized on Cu(513) facets. By combining complementary microscopy and spectroscopy techniques with theoretical calculations, we show the quasi-semiconducting character of the P-derived electronic states of the skewed-P overlayer, in contrast to the case of hexagonal phosphorene. The coexistence of these two competing structures gives rise to electronic P band modulation overlayer across the substrate while, locally, self-aligned nanoarrays of alternating hexagonal and skewed-square phosphorus terraces form. These results establish crystal-facet engineering as a practical route for discovering and stabilizing emergent 2D phases on high-index substrates.

item.title: Stacking-Directed Polarization and Excitonic Engineering in MoS$_2$/MoSe$_2$ van der Waals Heterostructures
item.description: arXiv:2606.22014v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The stacking-dependent polarization and excitonic response of MoS$_2$/MoSe$_2$ heterostructures were investigated using GW+BSE many-body perturbation theory. While homobilayer MoS$_2$ exhibited a switchable interlayer dipole driven by registry-induced symmetry breaking, the MoS$_2$/MoSe$_2$ hetero-interface remained pinned by the intrinsic chemical potential mismatch between sulfur and selenium. In 2L-MoS$_2$/MoSe$_2$ trilayers, the stacking sequence enabled a deterministic control of photogenerated electrons between the central and bottom MoS$_2$ layers, governed by internal electric fields and quasiparticle band-edge shifts of 60--70~meV. Our calculations predicted a 36~meV interlayer excitonic shift, in remarkable agreement with recent experiments. These results elucidate the microscopic link between atomic registry and many-body interactions, establishing transition metal dichalcogenide trilayers as a potential platform for sliding ferroelectricity and programmable optoelectronic functionalities.

item.title: Local magnetic correlations and light-sensitive centers in the Cr2AlC MAX phase
item.description: arXiv:2607.15110v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Cr2AlC MAX phase is synthesized by high-pressure solid-state annealing and investigated as a candidate platform for optically responsive magnetism. Structural characterization confirms the formation of the Cr2AlC phase, while magnetic and optical-magnetic properties are examined by superconducting quantum interference device (SQUID) magnetometry, electron spin resonance (ESR), and first principles calculations. SQUID magnetometry identifies Cr 2AlC as a weak, field-linear metallic paramagnet dominated by Pauli-like susceptibility of itinerant Cr-derived states. Its non-monotonic temperature dependence is described by an additional contribution from antiferromagnetically coupled Cr-Cr dimers, whereas the low-temperature Curie-like upturn originates from only a trace population of localized Cr centers. Under red-light illumination, SQUID magnetometry does not reveal an intrinsic macroscopic optomagnetic response. In contrast, ESR at 4 K shows a reversible light-induced reduction of a local magnetic signal, but the optically modified spin population corresponds only to several tens of ppm of the Cr sublattice. Ab initio Bethe-Salpeter equation (ai-BSE) calculations combined with the maximally localized Wannier function analysis suggest that optical excitation can redistribute spin polarization between neighboring Cr sites with the opposite local moments. The combined experiment-theory approach therefore establishes the hierarchy of magnetic contributions in Cr 2AlC and identifies the microscopic origin of its local optical sensitivity.

item.title: Uncertainty-quantified $J$-integral computation for quasicontinuum and finite element methods
item.description: arXiv:2607.23003v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The $J$-integral is a fundamental concept in fracture mechanics, quantifying the energy release rate that drives crack propagation. This work presents a rigorous implementation and validation of the $J$-integral within the multiscale three-dimensional (3D) quasicontinuum (QC3D) method, along with an uncertainty quantification analysis applicable to both QC3D and conventional FE methods. We compute the 3D $J$-integral under plane-strain assumptions, utilizing continuum mechanics fields (stress and strain energy density) derived from the underlying interatomic potential through the Cauchy--Born rule. Our implementation is comprehensively validated against both linear elastic fracture mechanics (LEFM) theory and the virtual crack extension (VCE) method for three regimes of increasing complexity: small-strain elasticity, and nonlinear deformation without and with atomic relaxation in the region near the crack tip. Excellent agreement is demonstrated in all cases. Further, we introduce a novel Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) framework to statistically assess the uncertainty in $J$-integral results for a given mesh and integration domain in QC3D and conventional FE methods. Our implementation's predictive capability is demonstrated through a QC3D simulation of a three-point bending test on silicon, where the computed critical energy release rate is shown to be in excellent agreement with the Griffith criterion. This work establishes a reliable and efficient framework for evaluating crack driving forces in multiscale fracture simulations with quantified uncertainty, enabling large-scale fracture simulations while resolving atomistic mechanisms at the crack tip.

item.title: Synthesis and structural validation of close-to-stoichiometric NiTe$_2$ single crystals
item.description: arXiv:2608.02334v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We report the synthesis of close-to-stoichiometric NiTe$_{2}$ single crystals via chemical vapor transport together with precise structural characterization. A combined analysis using powder and single crystal X-ray diffraction (XRD) was performed to determine lattice parameters and structural details. High-resolution single crystal XRD reveals no evidence of interstitial nickel, confirming a close-to-stoichiometric composition. This work establishes a reliable benchmark for the crystal structure of NiTe$_{2}$, offering a reference for future studies on its physical properties.
item.dc:creator: T. Tirasutt, L. H. Tjeng, A. C. Komarek

item.title: AutoXRD: Autonomous Large Language Model Agents and Comprehensive Evaluation for Powder X-Ray Diffraction Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2609.00070v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) is a foundational technique for structural and phase characterization in materials science, yet automating its analysis and evaluating it end-to-end remains challenging. Doing so requires an agent to interpret diffraction patterns, run refinement software, manage strongly coupled parameters in a physically meaningful order, and assess both numerical fit quality and physical validity. We propose AutoXRD, an LLM agent framework that organizes powder XRD analysis into refinement stages, uses diffraction diagnostics to select actions, and checks the resulting fits against crystallographic and physical criteria. We further introduce XRDBench with two complementary tracks. XRDBench-QA contains 100 tasks assessing scientific reasoning and decision-making, whereas XRDBench-E2E contains 34 end-to-end workflows requiring data interpretation, crystallographic software execution, iterative refinement, evidence preservation, and reporting. Across 1,340 runs of ten recent LLMs, models average only 57.8 out of 100, falling from 61.9 on XRDBench-QA to 53.7 on XRDBench-E2E. At the task level, they perform best on refinement-history assessment and result acceptance, but remain substantially weaker on refinement-action selection, phase quantification, indexing, and Rietveld refinement. Among individual models, GPT-5.6 Sol achieves the highest overall score of 81.1, GPT-5.6 Terra scores highest on XRDBench-E2E (81.0), and GPT-5.6 Luna provides the best score-cost trade-off. Moreover, ablations confirm that all six AutoXRD components consistently improve performance. Finally, execution-trace analysis reveals recurring failures in coupled-parameter control, quantitative reasoning, evidence preservation, and workflow termination, motivating stronger scientific constraints, uncertainty quantification, and more efficient planning.
item.dc:creator: Yuetong Wu, Maojun Sun

item.title: ZStar: A unified toolkit for polarization, Born effective charges, dielectric and piezoelectric responses, and infrared and Raman spectra
item.description: arXiv:2609.16802v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Polarization and the response to atomic displacements determine the dielectric, piezoelectric, and vibrational spectroscopy of materials, yet these quantities are usually obtained through separate workflows within ABACUS. Here, we present ZStar, an open-source Python toolkit that unifies these calculations. Using ABACUS and PYATB, ZStar derives Born effective charges (BECs) and zone-center force constants from one symmetry-adapted displacement set, and reuses the displaced electronic matrices for Raman spectra. Berry phases in periodic directions combined with charge-density dipoles in nonperiodic directions extend the method from bulk crystals (3D) to 2D and 1D materials and molecules (0D). These BECs and phonon modes give infrared intensities and the lattice contribution to the dielectric response. From finite strains, ZStar further obtains clamped-ion and relaxed-ion piezoelectric coefficients. This unified workflow reduces the computational cost by up to 4.2$\times$ for BECs and zone-center phonons and 8.4$\times$ for combined infrared and Raman calculations. ZStar also supports machine-learned models by generating training data and post-processing prediction results into physical properties.
item.dc:creator: Xudong Zhu, Junhong Li, Gan Jin, Zheng Guan, Meng Zhang, Lixin He

item.title: Quantum effects on the Peierls stress for screw dislocations in {\alpha}-Fe
item.description: arXiv:2611.27176v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The large discrepancy between the Peierls stress calculated using atomistic methods and that measured in experimental studies is well known. Despite significant research efforts over the past decades, our understanding of this mismatch remains limited. This work presents a multiscale study on the kinetics of screw dislocations in {\alpha}-Fe at 0.7K, employing the phonon description of temperature and using the Concurrent Atomistic-continuum (CAC) method as the simulation tool. Our simulations are shown to preserve the Bose-Einstein distribution of phonon modes and reproduce the nucleation and propagation of kink pairs. Large-scale CAC simulations with dislocation line lengths ranging from 0.1 to 2.1 microns, a typical range of lengths for screw dislocation lines, are performed, providing a quantitative and mechanistic understanding of the phonon-dislocation in {\alpha}-Fe. The experimentally measured Peierls stress in {\alpha}-Fe has been successfully reproduced, and the quantum effects on Peierls stress are quantified. Dependencies of phonon-dislocation interactions on dislocation line length and specimen size are explored and discussed.
item.dc:creator: Jiaqi Sun, Yang Li, Boyang Gu, David McDowell, Youping Chen

item.title: Collineations of particles as a tool to study nucleation and crystallization processes in liquids
item.description: arXiv:2611.29360v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We suggest several methods that can be used for identification of crystal nuclei in the studies of the nucleation and crystallization processes in multicomponent systems and in situations when the forming crystalline phase is different from the FCC, HCP or BCC lattices. The approaches are based on consideration of collineations of particles. They allow finding nuclei and separating them from each other. We demonstrate the methods by considering two systems. For a single-component system, we perform a comparison between the results derived from the collineations and those obtained using the coarse-grained bond-orientational order parameters. Further, we illustrate the methods by considering the crystallization process in a Wahnstr\"{o}m binary $BA_2$ system forming a rather complex crystal structure.
item.dc:creator: V. A. Levashov

item.title: Hierarchical Deep Research for Physically Grounded System-Level Materials Design
item.description: arXiv:2511.18303v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Designing multicomponent materials systems requires evidence on composition, interfaces, processing and deviceoperation that is scattered across the literature. Language-model research agents can collect this evidence, but their reports are seldom tested against physics. Here we show that Deep Tree of Research, a hierarchical multi-agent system built on locally deployable open-weight language models, ranks first among 47 agents in blinded evaluationacross 27 nanomaterials and device topics. Candidates from local agents outperform those from the best commercial systems on nine of ten first-principles simulation metrics across five design tasks. In a sensing case study, the agent nominated a fluorinated silver-nanoparticle/MXene architecture for the short-chain pollutant perfluoropentanoic acid; after an expert replaced the anchor with an amine, fabricated sensors respond selectively and reproduciblyintap water, consistent with interfacial calculations. Hierarchical research agents can therefore turn dispersed literatureinto experimentally testable materials hypotheses under human supervision.

item.title: Geometric Structure of Defects in General Teleparallel Geometry
item.description: arXiv:2602.01408v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We develop a curvature-free geometric framework for the description of topological defect structures. In conventional metric-affine models, dislocations are associated with torsion, disclinations with curvature, and point defects with non-metricity. However, this identification leads to a structural overlap in the defect classification, while curvature-squared metric formulations may also involve higher-order field equations. In this work we reformulate the defect variables within general teleparallel geometry, characterized by the vanishing of the total curvature, $R^a{}_b = 0$, while allowing nontrivial torsion and non-metricity. Within this setting, a reduced set of effective defect variables is constructed from selected components of the non-Riemannian field strengths. The torsion trace is adopted as an effective Burgers-type variable, the second trace of non-metricity as an effective Frank-type variable, and the first trace of non-metricity as a point-defect variable, while the scalar torsion component remains as an additional independent sector. The resulting structure defines a constrained geometric field system that admits a metric formulation. Quadratic Lagrangians constructed from torsion and non-metricity lead to second-order field equations in the teleparallel metric formulation considered here, without requiring curvature-squared terms. The framework provides a reduced geometric classification of effective defect fields and clarifies their underlying variational structure.
item.dc:creator: Muzaffer Adak, Ertan Kok, Mehmet Orhan

item.title: Short-range spin correlations and temperature-driven interlayer exchange crossover in the van der Waals magnet CrCl$_3$
item.description: arXiv:2607.09421v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We investigate the evolution of spin correlations and the nature of the multi-stage magnetic transition in the quasi-two-dimensional easy-plane van der Waals magnet $\rm CrCl_3$. By combining broadband magnetic resonance spectroscopy and DC SQUID magnetometry on mechanically exfoliated microflakes with non-local dynamical mean-field theory (DFT+DMFT) calculations, we analyze both long- and short range magnetic order in CrCl$_3$. Experimentally, SQUID and magnetic resonance measurements confirm the presence of the crossover to a spin polarized phase with the subsequent transition into an antiferromagnetic ground state upon cooling, but show robust short-range correlations at temperatures far above the magnetic ordering temperatures. Theoretically, we show the existence of highly stable local magnetic moments at room temperature, with a giant room temperature lifetime $\tau$ of 130--300 ps due to a wide Mott bandgap. Below room temperature, a rapid growth of the in-plane correlation length $\xi$ signals the formation of strong short range magnetic order consistent with the experimental observations. We also obtain a temperature-driven crossover of the interlayer exchange interaction, which changes from positive (ferromagnetic) at high temperatures to negative (antiferromagnetic) in the low-temperature ordered phase.
item.dc:creator: T. B. Mazitov, M. I. Panin, A. S. Pakhomov, M. V. Bakhmetiev, E. O. Chiglintsev, A. I. Chernov, A. A. Katanin

item.title: Electrothermal control of spin-reorientation transition in Co/Fe_3GaTe_2 heterostructures
item.description: arXiv:2607.15844v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Electrical control of magnetic anisotropy in van der Waals (vdWs) magnets is a key step toward reconfigurable two-dimensional spintronics, yet how a conventional metallic ferromagnet competes with a van der Waals magnet across a direct interface has remained largely unexplored. Here we demonstrate reversible thermal and electrothermal control of a spin-reorientation transition in Co/Fe_3GaTe_2 (FGaT) heterostructures. As Joule heating weakens the FGaT anisotropy, the heterostructure switches from an out-of-plane- to an in-plane-dominated state at a reorientation temperature of approximately 311 K, well below the Curie temperature, consistent with an exchange-mediated anisotropy competition between the Co overlayer and FGaT. An electrically driven device shows a closely matching loop evolution within an 80-100 mW power window, reversibly over five measurement cycles, consistent with an electrothermal origin. In a Co-free FGaT device, Kerr microscopy traces the switching to a power-tunable domain nucleation barrier and demonstrates power-thresholded, field-assisted magnetization reversal at a threshold near 15 mW. These results demonstrate electrothermal anisotropy competition as a route to heat-assisted and device-level control of vdWs magnetism.
